messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Adebayo was twenty years old, a pharmacist at a downtown clinic, and she had been in the United States for just over three years. She came to therapy reluctantly, referred by her supervisor after she had frozen mid-shift, staring at a sink full of water, unable to move or speak for nearly two minutes. Her coworkers thought she was having a seizure. Adebayo knew she was back in the room.

The room was a concrete cell in the basement of a government building in her home country. She had been detained for her family’s political affiliations—her older brother had been a student organizer, and when he fled, they took her instead. For three days, men she could not identify held her under. They forced her head into a barrel of water, over and over, until her lungs burned and her legs kicked uselessly against the floor. She remembered the sound of water sloshing, the cold shock against her scalp, and the way her body seized when she could not breathe. She remembered the metal taste of fear. She did not remember how it ended. The last guard left, and she was simply there, on the wet concrete, alone. Other prisoners in nearby cells had not been so lucky. She knew that because she heard them. She heard them stop making noise. She told herself she should have been the one who stopped.

Now, when a memory came, it was not a story she could tell. It was a position. Her back would arch, her hands would clench, and her neck would strain as if someone were pressing her face downward. She would feel the cold floor against her cheek, the weight of a hand on the back of her head, and she could not speak. Words did not belong to that memory. The memory belonged to her body, and her body did not have a language.

She had learned to avoid anything that might bring on those moments. She would not wash dishes at home because the sound of running water made her chest tighten. She stopped showering at night, because the dark and the steam together felt too close. She avoided the breakroom at work if anyone was arguing, because raised voices made her stomach drop and her eyes dart for an exit. She had come to believe that if she let herself think about what happened, even for a second, she would shatter completely—that the memory would swallow her and she would not come back. So she pushed it away, kept her mind busy, stayed in motion. But the pushing took a toll. She could not fall asleep at night without her back against the wall, facing the door, listening. She had to know every way out of every room before she could sit down. She scanned the faces of customers, checking for anyone who looked like the men from the basement. She had started arriving late to work because she could not bring herself to walk through the parking lot without checking every car, every shadow.

Her boyfriend, a kind man who knew only fragments of her story, had begun to pull away. He did not understand why she flinched when he touched her neck, or why she insisted on sleeping with the light on. She told him she was fine. She told herself she deserved the sleeplessness. She told herself she deserved the fear. Some nights, lying rigid beside him, she whispered that she should have been the one who did not make it out. The guilt was not a thought she could argue with—it was a fact, as solid as the floor beneath her.

What finally brought her to the clinic was not the guilt, or the scanning, or the way her body reenacted the drowning when she least expected it. It was the moment at the sink, when her supervisor had to shake her shoulder to bring her back, and she saw real fear in her coworker’s eyes. Adebayo realized she could no longer hide what was happening inside her. She was afraid of being seen, but she was more afraid of what might happen if she kept pretending nothing was wrong. She wanted to stop feeling like she was still in that room. She wanted to sleep without watching the door. She wanted to believe, for the first time in three years, that she was allowed to be alive.
